extracted.intended_audience: attorneys practicing before the USPTO, OED staff, and parties in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings and appeals (definitions of misconduct, procedural rules, statute of limitations, evidentiary standard, and sanctioning factors). Targeted to assessing attorney conduct before the USPTO and deciding appropriate discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect — 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits a practitioner from neglecting a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner; 'neglect' defined as 'the omission of proper attention to a person or thing, whether inadvertent, negligent, or willful.' Neglect generally requires a pattern or course of conduct and a time element; a single forgetful moment or honest mistake normally will not constitute neglect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time element is central; find neglect where practitioner 'ignores or otherwise disregards his obligations' and engages in inaction, delay, or lack of effort over months/years. Examples from the record: failing to monitor an application for two years, ignoring examiner phone calls, ignoring numerous client emails/calls, failing to associate application with customer number or use PAIR. Any one isolated misstep may not suffice, but a course of conduct can. (Citations and factual examples appear throughout the decision.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform client of important USPTO correspondence — 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner is required to inform a client when the practitioner receives correspondence from USPTO that could have a significant impact on a pending matter and a reasonable practitioner would believe the client should be notified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informing is more than mere notification. The practitioner must provide the document, fully explain its substance and ramifications (including relevant deadlines), and identify material consequences (e.g., claims objected to, claims that could be allowable if rewritten, deadlines to respond or appeal). Failing to attach the correspondence, failing to explain that certain claims needed rewriting, or failing to mention a deadline can constitute misconduct. Shifting blame to a client for not asking is not a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gross or disreputable conduct — 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) and (b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of the subsections of § 10.23 (such as § 10.23(c)(8)) automatically implicate § 10.23(a) and (b), which address gross or disreputable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding that the practitioner failed to inform the client of important correspondence or otherwise breached § 10.23(c) supports a legal conclusion of gross or disreputable conduct under § 10.23(a)/(b). The decision treats violations of (c) as giving rise, as a matter of law, to violations of (a) and (b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to seek lawful objectives / carry out contract of employment — 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(1) & (2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits failing to seek a client's lawful objectives and failing to carry out a contract of employment for professional services; these provisions emphasize consequences rather than intent and do not require intentional conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect that derails a client's objectives is sanctionable under § 10.84(a). Examples include unilateral decisions that foreclose options (e.g., not rewriting claims that could be made allowable) and failure to take available steps (e.g., failing to petition to revive) due to inadequate docketing or missed correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to deliver client property upon request — 37 C.F.R. § 10.112(c)(4)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must promptly deliver to a client, upon request, any client property in the practitioner's possession that the client is entitled to receive; a client's file is the client's property and must be returned on request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal circumstances (e.g., marital disputes, files physically located in the home) do not excuse the practitioner's duty. Reasonable efforts (e.g., subpoenaing documents, seeking access) are expected; failure to take such steps supports a finding of misconduct. Credibility issues about the practitioner's account of the file's whereabouts are relevant to the assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors for exclusion or suspension — 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(1)-(4)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ALJ initial decision imposing exclusion or suspension must explain the reason for imposing such sanction after considering four factors: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision must analyze each factor and explain how it supports the chosen sanction. Examples of application: evaluating duty breach severity, distinguishing negligent vs. intentional acts (e.g., intentional refusal to communicate), quantifying harm (monetary loss, lost opportunity to appeal), and weighing aggravators (disciplinary history) and mitigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing violations doctrine (timing of duty and statute of limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty to inform a client of potentially adverse information remains active until the practitioner informs the client of the correspondence or ceases representation of that client; violations that are not 'point in time' may be treated as continuing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the continuing violations theory, the statute of limitations may run from the date representation ends rather than the date of first alleged omission. Application affects timeliness of disciplinary complaints: if omissions continue, the misconduct may be timely under a later limitations period. The decision applies this doctrine to determine when the statutory clock began to run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations for USPTO disciplinary proceedings — 28 U.S.C. § 2462 (pre-AIA) and amended 35 U.S.C. § 32 (post-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to September 16, 2011, attorney discipline matters were governed by 28 U.S.C. § 2462 (a 5-year limitations period from accrual). The AIA (Leahy-Smith America Invents Act) amended the statute (now 35 U.S.C. § 32) to a two-stage limitation: proceedings must be commenced not later than the earlier of either 10 years after the date misconduct occurred, or 1 year after the date the misconduct is made known to an officer or employee of the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new § 32 applies to cases not already lapsed when the AIA took effect. Determination of which limitations regime applies depends on when the misconduct accrued and whether continuing violations extend accrual. Complaints must be evaluated against the applicable 5-year or 10/1-year standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director must prove alleged misconduct by clear and convincing evidence in disciplinary proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites that the OED Director provided clear and convincing evidence of the practitioner's failures (e.g., failure to monitor docket, ignoring client communications). Application of this standard affects whether factual findings and misconduct determinations are sustained on review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirement to cite administrative record for proposed changes to findings — 37 C.F.R. § 11.55
rubrics_metrics.description: A party proposing changes to an ALJ's findings of fact on review must cite support in the administrative record as required by 37 C.F.R. § 11.55.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to cite record evidence for proposed alterations to findings supports rejection of those proposed changes. Rejections throughout the decision rely on appellant's failure to cite the administrative record in accordance with § 11.55.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (ABA Standards guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining sanctions, the ALJ and reviewing officer should identify aggravating and mitigating factors, following guidance from the ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical aggravating factors include prior disciplinary history (particularly similar prior misconduct), intentionality, harm to client, attempts to silence or obstruct, and repeated offenses. Mitigating factors (fewer here) may include personal circumstances but are weighed against severity and recurrence. The decision identifies six aggravators and two mitigators and relies on ABA Standards (e.g., Standards § 9.2) to calibrate sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Docket management and communication system obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are expected to maintain reasonable docket-management practices and communication systems (associate customer numbers, maintain accurate address of record, use PAIR or equivalent, maintain tickler systems), and not to delegate critical mail handling without protection against loss of critical correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor office procedures (using an executive suite without reliable mail receipt, relying on an untrained receptionist to sort critical mail, failing to associate customer number, lacking a tickler system) are negligent and can support findings of misconduct. Remedies/expectations include associating customer ID, using PAIR, updating address of record, and implementing reliable calendaring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission to Committee on Discipline as prerequisite to filing complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission of a disciplinary matter to the Committee on Discipline is a procedural prerequisite to filing a formal OED complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.22 and 11.23 impose no requirements on the content of what the OED Director submits to the Committee, submission is required before a complaint is filed; the timing of submissions and subsequent malpractice dismissal can be relevant to procedural history but do not affect USPTO jurisdiction if Committee submission occurred.
